uncited: This family encompasses methods that generate a voxel representation of 3D geometry by leveraging standard 2D rasterization hardware or libraries.

Instead of performing explicit geometric intersection tests against a 3D voxel grid, these methods project the input primitives onto 2D planes, rasterize them to determine coverage, and map the results back to 3D voxel coordinates.

This approach distinguishes itself from siblings like [Binary Volume Rendering](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) and [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by relying on the efficiency of established 2D rasterization pipelines rather than brute-force 3D traversal or simple thresholding.
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of decoupling the rasterization step from the final 3D grid storage or utilizing 2D buffers as an intermediate representation.
**Projection:** Mapping 3D input primitives (typically triangles) onto a 2D domain (either a projection plane or a UV space).
**Rasterization:** Using a 2D rasterizer to determine which pixels/texels are covered by the primitives.
**Mapping:** Converting the 2D coverage information into 3D voxel indices.
This may involve evaluating depth at pixel centers, storing face IDs for later interpolation, or using union-based hash tables to resolve overlaps.
**Aggregation:** Combining results from multiple passes (e.g., three axes) or chunks into a final voxel set.
The specific implementation details, such as whether to use 6-separating or 26-separating connectivity, and how to handle memory for large meshes, vary by child method.
The use of rasterization for voxelization leverages the maturity and speed of 2D graphics pipelines to solve 3D geometric problems.
This approach avoids the computational overhead of explicit 3D intersection tests.

The specific variants within this family have been developed to address limitations in memory usage (chunking), connectivity requirements (6-axis vs 26-axis), and overlap resolution (union-based hashing).
